notes: Sample app_commands.json - what the scheduler runs. Copy to app_commands.json and edit. The daemon reads this file and starts each active entry as its own process on its own interval; nothing here is compiled in, so an app is added, retimed or switched off by editing data.

'working_dir' is the literal string 'tools/db_ops' on every entry and is NOT a folder on your disk. It is a logical alias for the tool root, resolved at run time to wherever the project actually lives - a flat checkout on a workstation, or /app/tools/db_ops inside the container - so the same file works on both.

'time_window' is the shared scheduling object used across the whole toolkit. Null bounds mean no restriction; from_hour/to_hour confine a command to a window; 'repeat_interval' is seconds between runs, counted from the PREVIOUS run's start, so a command taking 9s with an interval of 10 becomes due 1s after it exits.
'repeat_interval': 0 means run once and leave it running - that is how a server that stays up (the web host) is expressed. 'repeat_interval': -1 means manual only: never scheduled, run on request.

'timeout' must stay ABOVE the slowest thing the command does, not merely above the average. A collection pass killed at its timeout loses every metric in it, not just the slow one - worse than the slow metric failing alone. A command still running when its interval comes round is skipped, not started twice.
'log_scope' names the log files the run writes: logs/<log_scope>.log and logs/<log_scope>_runtime.log.
'node_role' limits an entry to a node started with that role (DB_OPS_NODE_ROLE). One config file can then be shipped everywhere without a machine running the apps it has no access for.
Start small. A first install usually runs only APP-METRICS until the targets and credentials are proven, then adds reports and delivery.

app_commands.note: The timeout is the budget for a whole pass, so it stays above the largest single metric timeout in metric_definitions.json plus the rest of the pass. Equal is not enough - the slow metric would still be running when the daemon reached its own limit.

app_commands._note: This entry only decides how often the reports app WAKES UP. Which reports are due is decided in data/reports_config.json - two levels on purpose, so adding a report does not mean touching the scheduler.
Inactive in this example because a fresh install has no SQL tasks defined yet. Turning it on with an empty sql_commands.json is harmless - it simply finds nothing due.
--allow-fail means a failing objective is reported, not treated as a broken command. Without it every SLO breach would also read as a scheduler failure, and those are different facts.

app_commands.display_name: Deliver the queue and answer commands
app_commands._note: One second, because this is the interactive path: it delivers one queued message and processes one incoming command per pass. Leave it inactive until telegram_config.json is enabled and the groups are confirmed.

app_commands.display_name: Serve the rendered reports over HTTP
app_commands.command_text: python -m db_ops.webhost.cli --config config.json serve --root runtime/reports --mount report_dba --port 8080
app_commands._note: repeat_interval 0 = run once and keep running. The daemon starts it, sees it is still alive on every later pass, and does not start a second one.
